claims.text: Surface atomic disorder and elemental segregation primarily govern the onset and progression of premelting and melting in initially solid FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Surface disorder and segregation lower the local melting point of the nanoparticle surface relative to the core.
High configurational entropy and chemical complexity enhance the surface-mediated melting-point depression.
FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles melt gradually from the surface inward rather than through an abrupt bulk transition.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles have uniform elemental composition.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are crystalline solids.
Heating through the premelting and melting regime induces surface atomic disorder and elemental segregation at the nanoparticle interface.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles promotes surface atomic rearrangement and segregation.
The multicomponent character of high-entropy alloys promotes surface atomic rearrangement and segregation.
Increased local disorder reduces the energy barrier for surface-atom mobility.
Reduced barriers to surface-atom mobility produce a lower surface melting temperature.
As temperature rises, surface premelting initiates and propagates inward before the core melts.
The nanoparticle core melts at a higher temperature than the surface.
FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will show a lower onset temperature for surface premelting than bulk material or larger particles.
Surface atomic mobility or disorder will become detectable before complete particle melting.
The nanoparticle melting transition will be broader than that of bulk FeNiCrCoCu or particles larger than 100 nm.
Elemental surface segregation may become detectable before complete melting.
Bulk FeNiCrCoCu or particles larger than 100 nm exhibit a sharper, higher-temperature melting transition with minimal surface premelting.
The proposed mechanism applies to 5–20 nm FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles under an inert atmosphere.
Particle sizes below 3 nm or above 50 nm and reactive atmospheres may produce deviations from the proposed behavior.
